title: Number of Divisible Triplet Sums
statement: You are given an integer array `nums` and an integer `d`. Count the index triplets `(i, j, k)` with `i < j < k` for which `nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k]` is a multiple of `d`, and return that count. Triplets are told apart by their indices, so equal values at different positions form different triplets; an array with fewer than three elements has none.
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every triplet is O(n³), too slow for 1,000 elements. Divisibility only depends on remainders: once two of the numbers are fixed, the third must have one specific remainder modulo `d`. So fix the middle index `j` and the last index `k`, and look up how many earlier indices `i < j` have the remainder that completes the sum. A hash map from remainder to count of the elements before `j` answers that in O(1).

## Approach

1. Keep `seen`, mapping each remainder `nums[i] % d` to how many indices `i` before the current `j` have it.
2. For each `j`, loop over every `k > j`. The first number must have remainder `need = (d - (nums[j] + nums[k]) % d) % d`; add `seen.get(need)` to `total`.
3. After all `k` for this `j`, record `nums[j] % d` in `seen`, so it can serve as `i` for later middles.
4. Return `total`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [3, 3, 4, 7, 8]`, `d = 5`.

- `j = 0`: `seen` is empty, nothing counted; then remainder 3 is stored.
- `j = 1`: pair with `k = 2` has sum 7, `need = 3`, one match (index 0), `total = 1`. Pairs with 7 and 8 need 2 and 4: none. Remainder 3 now has count 2.
- `j = 2`: pair (4, 8) sums to 12, `need = 3`, two matches, `total = 3`. Pair (4, 7) needs 4: none.
- `j = 3`: pair (7, 8) needs 0: none. The answer is `3`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n²): every pair `(j, k)` is visited once with an O(1) lookup.
- Space: O(min(n, d)) for the remainder map.

## Pitfalls

- Values reach 10^9, so `nums[j] + nums[k]` can be 2·10^9 and a three-value sum 3·10^9: in Java or C use 64-bit arithmetic or reduce modulo `d` first.
- The outer `% d` in `need` turns a remainder of `d` back into 0 when the pair sum is already divisible.
- Add `nums[j]` to `seen` only after its inner loop; adding it earlier would let `i` equal `j`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `seen` | count of each remainder among indices before `j` |
| `j`, `k` | middle and last index of the triplet |
| `need` | remainder the first number must have |
| `rem` | remainder of `nums[j]`, stored for later |
| `total` | number of valid triplets found |

narration.2: seen counts the remainders of the elements to the left of the current middle index.
narration.3: total accumulates the number of valid triplets.
narration.5: Fix j as the middle index of the triplet.
narration.6: Try every k after j as the last index.
narration.7: Work out which remainder the first number must have for the three to sum to a multiple of d.
narration.8: Every earlier index with that remainder completes a valid triplet, so add their count.
narration.10: Take the remainder of nums[j] modulo d.
narration.11: Only now record it, so it acts as the first index for later middles and never pairs with itself.
narration.13: Every (j, k) pair has been matched with its valid first indices; return the count.
